The panel is checking the link between the MBA and your plan. State your long-term goal first, then the gaps in skills, knowledge and network that stand between you and it, and then show how specific parts of the MBA close each gap.

Example: "My long-term goal is to [lead a function/start a venture/become a head of X]. Today I lack [finance and strategy depth, cross-functional exposure, leadership practice]. The MBA gives me those through [core courses, case work, electives, internships, peer network]. After the MBA I will start as [role] and grow towards [goal]." Keep it realistic and consistent with your earlier answers.

The panel challenges your reasons for leaving a rewarding job, so do not criticise the job. Acknowledge that it is good, then explain why it is not enough for your long-term goal: your growth in this field will be limited to [domain], whereas your ambition lies in [function, industry, general management], which needs broader business skills.

A sample: "My current role has been rewarding, and I have learnt a lot. But I want to move from [executing] to [deciding and leading], and for that I need [finance, strategy, people management] and exposure to other industries. The MBA is the right way to build that, and I see it as a long-term investment, not a short-term salary move." Show clarity, not dissatisfaction.

This is a standard request to describe your past roles. For each organisation, give the designation and period, the team or function, two or three main responsibilities, and one or two achievements with numbers. Then connect your learning to your MBA goals.

A structure: "At [organisation], I worked as [role] for [duration]. I was responsible for [tasks], worked with [stakeholders], and delivered [result]. Earlier at [organisation], I [role and outcome]." Keep each organisation to about 30 seconds, stay honest and be ready for deeper questions on any project you mention.

This question tests problem-solving and ownership. Choose one real project, and use a simple structure: the situation, the challenge, your action and the result, followed by a lesson.

Typical challenges in smart city or analytics projects include poor or messy data, unclear requirements from stakeholders, coordination among agencies, tight deadlines, resistance to change and integrating legacy systems. Example: "In [project], the data from [sources] was inconsistent, so I [cleaned and standardised it, set up a validation process and aligned stakeholders on definitions]. As a result we [delivered X, reduced time by Y]. I learnt that [lesson]." Use only a real example and quantify the result if possible.

Business analytics is a field or function that uses data, statistics and models to produce insights and support decisions. A business analyst is a role: someone who studies business needs, gathers and clarifies requirements, analyses processes and data, and works as a link between business stakeholders and technical teams to recommend solutions. In short, analytics is the discipline and the toolkit, whereas a business analyst is one job that may use it. Related roles are data analyst, data scientist and analytics manager, who focus more on data and models.

Then align it with your own experience: say what you have actually done, for example gathering requirements, building dashboards, or modelling, and which side of the spectrum your work falls on, and what you hope to learn.

The panel wants to know what you will bring, not just take. Look at your experience and pick two or three assets that are relevant to a student community: a domain such as analytics or government projects, leadership or event roles, mentoring juniors, technical skills you can share, or community activities.

Example: "My experience in [projects] has taught me [skills]. At IIM Amritsar I would like to contribute through [analytics club/case competitions/peer learning sessions], and bring a practitioner's perspective to class discussions on [topic]." Make the contribution concrete, and show humility by saying you also expect to learn from peers.

This question asks for practical examples of applying your knowledge. Choose one or two concrete instances and describe them using situation, action and result. Show how a technical idea (a statistical method, a model, a process-improvement tool) or a managerial idea (planning, delegation, stakeholder management) was used to solve a real problem.

For example: "During my internship at [company], I used [regression/forecasting/Excel modelling] to [predict demand/cut cost]. This led to [result]. It taught me that [lesson on translating theory into practice]." Avoid jargon-heavy answers without outcomes, and be ready for follow-up questions on your method.

Operations management concepts are applied in government projects in several ways. Project planning and scheduling tools such as Gantt charts and critical path method are used to sequence tasks and monitor timelines. Supply chain and inventory management apply to material procurement and public distribution. Capacity planning and resource allocation decide manpower, machinery and budgets. Quality management (inspection, standards, audits) is used to ensure works meet specifications, and process improvement and technology help reduce delays and leakages.

Challenges are procurement delays, land and clearance issues, multiple agencies and cost overruns, so concepts such as risk management, vendor management and real-time monitoring dashboards matter. Add one example from your own experience if you have it, such as a smart city project.

Prepare to explain each concept simply, with a business example. Probability is the measure of how likely an event is, between 0 and 1; for example, the chance of a customer buying after a click. Differentiation measures the rate of change of a quantity, such as marginal cost or marginal revenue, and finding where the derivative is zero helps in optimisation. Statistics is about collecting, summarising and drawing conclusions from data, using measures such as mean, variance and hypothesis tests.

Show how they relate to your field: for example, probability and statistics in forecasting and A/B testing, differentiation in optimisation of cost or profit. Start with a plain definition, then an example, and ask whether the panel wants more depth.

The pandemic accelerated digitisation, so data analytics became more central to how organisations operate. Firms used data for demand forecasting in volatile conditions, supply chain visibility, remote work and productivity tracking, healthcare and vaccine logistics, contact tracing and epidemic modelling, and personalised e-commerce and digital payments. Customer behaviour data became more valuable as more activity moved online.

The post-pandemic world is also more uncertain, so businesses need real-time insight, scenario planning and automation, and governments need data to target welfare and manage public health. Challenges include privacy, data quality, skills shortages and the risk of over-reliance on models. Conclude that analytics is now a basic part of competitive strategy, not an add-on.

The panel wants a detailed, structured account of one project you can discuss in depth. Choose the project that best shows your skills and impact, and use the structure: context and objective, your role, approach and tools, challenges, results, and implications or learning.

Example: "In [project], the objective was [goal]. I was responsible for [role]. We used [method], faced [challenge] and solved it by [action]. The outcome was [quantified result], which implied [wider impact, such as cost saving, better decisions, policy change]. The key lesson was [lesson]." Be ready for deep follow-ups on any number or method you mention.

Pros of electric vehicles are lower running costs per kilometre, zero tailpipe emissions and less urban air pollution, lower dependence on imported oil, quieter operation and fewer moving parts to maintain. Cons are higher upfront price, limited charging infrastructure and range anxiety, long charging times, battery cost, replacement and recycling, dependence on imported battery minerals and cells, and the fact that electricity in India is still largely coal-based, so the emission gain is partial.

Analytics can help by predicting demand and choosing optimal charger locations from traffic and usage data, optimising grid load and time-of-day pricing, estimating battery health and total cost of ownership for buyers, targeting subsidies and customer segments, and forecasting adoption. Conclude that analytics can lower the barriers that people actually face, such as range anxiety and cost uncertainty.

The question asks for an opinion on recent developments, so stay balanced and fact-based. On the Farm Laws of 2020, the government argued that they would give farmers freedom to sell outside mandis and attract private investment, while farmers, especially in Punjab and Haryana, feared the loss of assured MSP procurement and weaker bargaining power. After a year of protests, the laws were repealed in late 2021. The lesson is the importance of consultation and safeguards in reform.

Vaccine diplomacy refers to India supplying COVID-19 vaccines (Vaccine Maitri) to many countries, which improved its soft power, but it was criticised after the second wave when domestic supply was short. Present your view calmly and acknowledge both sides. Verify the details before the interview.

The Union Budget is the government's annual statement of expected receipts and expenditure. Structure your answer around its key focus areas: fiscal deficit targets and the borrowing plan, capital expenditure on infrastructure (roads, railways, ports), allocations for defence, health, education and agriculture, tax changes for individuals and corporates, and incentives such as production-linked schemes, MSME support and green energy.

Then add the implications for business: higher capex helps construction, cement, steel and capital goods; tax changes affect disposable income and consumption; fiscal discipline influences interest rates and the cost of capital; and incentives guide investment decisions. Use specific figures from the latest budget only if you are sure of them.

'Data is the new oil' means that data, like oil, is a raw resource that creates enormous value once refined and used. Companies such as Google, Meta and Amazon built huge businesses by collecting data, analysing it for insight and targeting customers, and data now drives decisions, AI models, personalised services and new products.

The analogy has limits and brings challenges: data is not used up when used, and it is only valuable when processed. The challenges include privacy and consent (India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023), security and breaches, bias in data and algorithms, data quality, concentration of power in a few firms, and data ownership. A balanced conclusion is that data creates value, but trust, regulation and responsible use are essential.

The panel is testing your awareness of key officeholders. Hold the main names and portfolios accurately, and always verify them just before the interview, because they change. Examples to cover: the Prime Minister, the Finance Minister (who presents the Union Budget and handles economic policy), the Commerce and Industry Minister, the External Affairs Minister, the Defence Minister, the Home Minister, and the RBI Governor, with the RBI Deputy Governors who handle areas such as monetary policy and regulation.

Be ready to say what each does in one line, for example that the RBI Governor leads monetary policy and chairs the Monetary Policy Committee. If you are unsure of a name, say so honestly rather than guess.

National policies shape industry through incentives, costs and regulation. Renewable energy initiatives, such as the National Solar Mission, the target of 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030, PLI schemes for solar modules and batteries, and green hydrogen plans, create new demand and investment opportunities in solar, wind, storage, EVs and power equipment, while pushing traditional fossil-based industries to adapt.

For the industry you work in, explain the effects in three parts: opportunities (new products, lower energy costs, subsidies), challenges (higher upfront investment, grid integration, supply chain dependence on imports) and the strategic response (efficiency, own renewable generation, new business lines). Tie it to your own sector with a specific example.

This is the standard opener and the panel is judging structure, clarity and confidence. Start with your name and background, and then give a tight summary of about 90 seconds: education, work experience or key achievements, one or two interests, and why you want the MBA.

Example: "I am [name], from [city]. I completed [degree] from [college] and worked as [role] at [company], where I [achievement]. Outside work I [hobby]. I am keen to pursue an MBA to [goal]." Do not recite your resume line by line, and leave two or three hooks that you are comfortable being questioned on.

Yes, you should always have one or two good questions, since it shows curiosity and preparation. Do not say 'no questions'. Ask something that is not answered on the website and that shows you have thought about your fit: how the programme supports students moving into a different function, how industry projects and live cases are integrated, what the panel sees as the traits of the most successful students, or how the institute plans to grow in your area of interest.

Avoid questions about salary guarantees or things easily found online. Keep it brief and polite, listen to the answer, and thank the panel.

This looks like a behavioural question in disguise, testing how you plan and prioritise. A good answer shows a structured habit: you research the destination, plan the itinerary and budget, book transport and stay, check documents and weather, make a packing list, and think about contingencies such as health, safety and local rules.

Tie it to a management skill: "I start with a checklist, because it helps me avoid last-minute surprises. That habit carries into my work, where I [plan projects with milestones and backups]." Keep it natural and genuine, and be ready with a short story about a trip that did not go to plan and how you handled it.

In basketball, a technical foul is a penalty for unsportsmanlike or non-contact misconduct rather than ordinary physical contact during play. Examples are arguing with or showing disrespect to a referee, using abusive language, delay of game, taunting, too many players on court, or hanging on the rim.

The opposing team gets one free throw (in the NBA, a shot by a player chosen by the coach) and usually possession of the ball. In the NBA, a player who receives two technical fouls in a game is ejected. Rules differ slightly between leagues, so mention the league if you are asked.

'Why MBA?' tests clarity of purpose. The panel wants a logical story rather than a slogan: where you are now, what gap you see, why an MBA is the right way to fill it, and what you will do afterwards.

Use a past-present-future structure. For example: "My experience in [field] showed me [limitation]. I want to build [finance, strategy, leadership skills], which an MBA provides through [case method, peers, electives]. After the programme, I aim to [short-term role] and later [long-term goal]." Avoid cliches such as 'higher salary' on its own, and link the answer to this particular institute.

Financial literacy, which covers budgeting, saving, credit, insurance, investing and understanding scams, is a life skill that most Indians learn late and often the hard way. Supporters argue that teaching it early builds good habits, protects people from fraud and debt traps, and supports financial inclusion at a time when digital payments and investing are growing fast.

Opponents argue that the curriculum is already heavy, that teachers may not be trained, and that abstract finance is hard for young children. A balanced view is that financial literacy deserves a place, but it should be done smartly: integrate simple, practical modules into existing subjects such as maths and social science, use activities and real-life examples, train teachers, and increase difficulty gradually. In conclusion, if designed well, it will help students more than burden them.

India's COVID-19 vaccination drive became one of the largest in the world in absolute numbers, with more than two billion doses administered, using the CoWIN digital platform, indigenous vaccines such as Covaxin and Covishield production, and a nationwide network of centres. Coverage was widespread across states, though there were early supply shortages, urban-rural and digital-access gaps, and vaccine hesitancy in some areas.

It differed from past drives such as polio and universal immunisation in that it targeted adults first by age group, needed cold-chain handling for a new vaccine, depended on digital registration, and was driven under extreme time pressure with a fast-moving virus, whereas earlier drives focused on children through established routine systems. Verify the latest numbers before quoting any.

India has one of the largest start-up ecosystems in the world, with over a hundred unicorns and tens of thousands of registered start-ups, concentrated in cities such as Bengaluru, Delhi NCR and Mumbai. Key factors include a large domestic market, a young and tech-savvy population, low-cost engineering talent, cheap mobile data and UPI-driven digital payments, growing venture capital, and policy support such as Startup India and the digital public infrastructure stack.

Is it accidental or intentional? It is a mixture: many conditions, like demographics and the mobile revolution, were favourable by chance, but government initiatives, investment in digital infrastructure, and a maturing investor and mentor network were deliberate. Challenges remain, such as funding slowdowns, regulatory clarity and profitability. Conclude that the emergence was helped by luck, but sustained by deliberate choices.

The proposal to raise the minimum marriage age for women from 18 to 21 aims to reduce early marriage and its effects on health, education and gender equality, and to align the age with that of men. Supporters say it would allow girls to complete education, delay early pregnancies, improve maternal and child health and increase women's workforce participation.

Critics argue that law alone will not change behaviour, since early marriage is driven by poverty, social norms and lack of schooling, and that it may criminalise marriages among poorer or marginalised families and push them underground, while child marriage laws already exist and are weakly enforced. A balanced conclusion is that it can help only if accompanied by education, scholarships, jobs, awareness and strong enforcement.

COVID-19 exposed gaps in health infrastructure, supply chains, data systems and global coordination. Whether the next pandemic can be prevented is a nuanced question: we cannot prevent every outbreak, because new pathogens will keep emerging from animals and from changing human contact with nature, but we can prevent an outbreak from becoming a pandemic.

The measures include strong disease surveillance and early warning systems, investment in public health infrastructure and trained staff, quick vaccine and diagnostic platforms, global data sharing and cooperation, stockpiles of essential supplies, and protecting ecosystems and regulating wildlife trade. A fair conclusion is that prevention in the strict sense is not guaranteed, but preparedness and rapid response can greatly reduce the damage, if the lessons are not forgotten.

An ageing population is a major social and economic challenge. As the share of the elderly increases, the burden on healthcare, pensions and caregiving rises, while the working-age share may shrink in the long run. Many elderly Indians lack pension coverage, face loneliness and depend on family support that is weakening with urbanisation.

Policy suggestions: expand universal health coverage with geriatric care and affordable long-term care services, strengthen social security through broader pension schemes and savings products, encourage active ageing through flexible work and skills programmes, develop age-friendly housing and public spaces, promote community and digital support systems, and invest in raising the productivity of the working population. Conclude that early planning is needed, so that this becomes a demographic opportunity, with experienced seniors contributing, not a crisis.

This is a simple factual question, and the panel may be checking a connection or a conflict of interest. Answer honestly and briefly: if you have a relative who studied here, name the relationship, the years and the programme, and mention what you learned about the institute from them, which also shows a genuine connection.

If not, say: "No sir, I do not, but I have learned about the institute through [alumni, website, seniors]." Do not make any claim that could be checked and found false.

The panel wants to know your standing and tests your honesty and decision-making. Answer directly: if you have an offer, name the company, role and the package range only if asked, and explain how it fits with your MBA plan. If you do not, say so calmly and explain what you are doing next.

A sample: "Yes sir, I have an offer from [company] as [role], and I have kept it as a backup, but my goal is to pursue an MBA to [reason]." If you have none: "No, I decided to prepare for MBA entrance full time." Do not exaggerate or speak negatively about the offer or your college.

The panel is testing the clarity of your reasons for going directly into an MBA. Accept that experience has value, then give your reasons: you have a clear career goal that needs the MBA early, you want to learn the fundamentals first and apply them across a longer career, you already have exposure through internships, projects or leadership roles, and you believe you will learn from peers while contributing from your own experience.

Example: "I understand that experience adds depth, and I have built some through [internships/projects]. But I am clear about my goal in [field], and I think the best time to build the foundation is now, so I can apply it for more years." Do not sound dismissive of experience.

Yes. A lithium-ion (Li-ion) battery is a rechargeable battery in which lithium ions move from the negative electrode (anode, usually graphite) to the positive electrode (cathode, a lithium metal oxide or phosphate) during discharge, and back during charging, through an electrolyte, while electrons flow through the external circuit and power the device.

Its advantages are high energy density, low self-discharge and long cycle life, which is why it is used in phones, laptops and electric vehicles. Its limitations are cost, safety (thermal runaway if damaged or overcharged), degradation over time, and dependence on lithium, cobalt and nickel. Common chemistries include NMC and LFP.

Prepare a structured answer. EVs date back to the 19th century, when early electric cars competed with steam and petrol, but petrol dominated due to cheap oil and range. Modern revival came with lithium-ion batteries, Toyota Prius hybrids and then Tesla. The US succeeded because of strong policy incentives, higher incomes, charging networks, early-adopter culture and investment in battery technology. India is growing more slowly because of high upfront cost, limited charging infrastructure, dependence on imported batteries, a price-sensitive market and grid concerns, though schemes like FAME and PLI are helping.

To convince a common man: lower running cost per kilometre, lower maintenance, fewer moving parts, rising fuel prices and subsidies, which together can offset the higher price over some years. Be honest about the limits, such as range and charging.

The power grid is the network that generates, transmits and distributes electricity. Power is generated at power plants (thermal, hydro, nuclear, solar, wind), stepped up to high voltage by transformers for transmission over long distances with low losses, and sent through high-voltage lines to substations, where it is stepped down and distributed to homes and industries at lower voltages.

The key challenge is balancing supply and demand in real time, as electricity cannot be stored easily, and frequency must remain stable at 50 Hz in India. Load dispatch centres coordinate generation, and India has a unified national grid. Renewable energy adds variability, which creates the need for storage, forecasting and flexible grids.

An induction motor has two main parts: the stator and the rotor. The stator is the stationary part, with a laminated steel core holding three-phase windings placed in slots, which creates a rotating magnetic field when supplied with three-phase AC. The rotor is the rotating part, and it is of two types: the squirrel cage rotor, with aluminium or copper bars short-circuited by end rings, and the wound rotor, with windings connected to slip rings.

The rotating magnetic field induces currents in the rotor, which produce torque, making the rotor follow the field at a speed slightly below synchronous speed (this difference is called slip). Squirrel-cage motors are simple, rugged and widely used in industry.

The panel has asked several personal questions that are linked to your form, so be prepared with honest, specific answers: your hobbies (powerlifting and reading), your competition results including the rank you got, your favourite authors and genres, and a one-line summary of the book Sapiens.

Sapiens by Yuval Noah Harari can be summed up in one line as a history of humankind that argues that our ability to believe in shared fictions, such as money, religion and nations, allowed Homo sapiens to cooperate at scale and dominate the world. For other anthropology books, only mention ones you have read, such as Guns, Germs and Steel by Jared Diamond or Homo Deus by Harari. Do not claim ranks or books that you cannot discuss.

The panel is asking about your internship and the approach you took. Describe the company and project briefly, the problem to be solved, your approach step by step (data collection, analysis method, tools), and the result. Then explain why you chose that approach over alternatives.

Example: "During my internship at [company], I worked on [problem]. I first [gathered data], then used [method such as regression, root cause analysis or a simulation] because [reason]. The outcome was [result]. If I did it again, I would [improvement]." Be honest about your role and ready for technical follow-up questions.

The panel wants a clear picture of your employer and role. Describe the company in two lines (industry, size, leadership position and what it is known for), explain how it leads, such as through market share, technology, brands or innovation, then state your exact designation, team and responsibilities.

A sample: "I work at [company], a leader in [industry], known for [strength]. My designation is [role] in [team], where I [responsibilities]. A key achievement was [result]." Be accurate about facts and numbers, and avoid exaggerating your seniority.

This question has two parts: why you changed jobs, and an example of problem-solving. For the first, give a positive, growth-based reason, such as wanting broader scope, learning, a new domain or better alignment with your goals, without criticising your previous employer. For the second, give a real example in the STAR format.

Example: "I changed from [company A] to [company B] because I wanted [bigger role/new skills]. At [company], when we faced [problem], I [analysed it, tried a solution, involved the team], and we achieved [result]." Keep the story honest and ensure that the reason for the switch connects to your MBA plans.

Yes, I can describe a model, with caution about its limits. To predict an election outcome, I would collect data such as past results by constituency, demographics, opinion polls, candidate profiles, local issues, turnout trends and social media signals. I would then use methods such as logistic regression or random forest for constituency-level winner prediction, or a Bayesian model that updates with new polls, and validate it on previous elections.

Do such models capture real sentiment? Only partly. Polls suffer from sampling and response bias, social media does not represent all voters, late swings and local factors are hard to capture, and models inherit the bias of the data. Therefore, predictions should be presented as probabilities, not certainties, and complemented with ground-level insight.

The panel is testing the strength of your motivation, since software engineering is well paid. Accept that it is a good career, and then explain why you want a different path: your interest in [business, product, strategy, leadership], the desire to move from building to deciding and managing, and the need for skills that an MBA gives, such as finance, strategy and people leadership.

Example: "Software engineering has been rewarding, but I find myself drawn to [problem framing/customer needs/business decisions]. An MBA will give me the broader toolkit to move into [product management/consulting], where I can have impact at a larger scale." Avoid giving money or status as the reason.

The panel wants a realistic and clear plan. Present it in stages: the short-term goal (the first role after the MBA, in a function and industry), the medium-term goal (growth within three to five years) and the long-term vision (the position or impact you want in ten years), and tie it to what you will learn.

Example: "After the MBA I plan to work as [role] in [industry], to build experience in [skills]. In five years I want to [lead a team/manage a product line], and in the long run [become a business head/start a venture]." Keep it consistent with your earlier answers and flexible enough to show maturity.

Monetary policy is the management of money supply and interest rates by the central bank (the RBI in India) to control inflation and support growth, using tools such as the repo rate, the cash reserve ratio, open market operations and liquidity operations. Fiscal policy is the government's use of taxation and spending (and borrowing) to influence the economy, set out in the Union Budget.

In short, the RBI handles money and credit, while the government handles taxes and expenditure. They should work together: for example, when inflation is high, the RBI may raise rates and the government may cut deficits. India's monetary policy follows an inflation target of 4 percent with a tolerance band of 2 to 6 percent.

The classic relationship is shown by the Phillips curve, which suggests an inverse relationship in the short run: when unemployment is low, wages and prices tend to rise faster, causing higher inflation, and when unemployment is high, inflation tends to be lower. This presents a trade-off for policymakers.

In the long run, the relationship breaks down, since expectations adjust. Economists such as Friedman and Phelps argued that there is a natural rate of unemployment, and the 1970s stagflation (high inflation with high unemployment) showed that the trade-off is not stable. Today the relationship is considered weaker and is affected by supply shocks, global factors and inflation expectations.

Valuing an asset means estimating what it is worth, based on the benefits it will provide. The main approaches are the income approach (discounted cash flows: the present value of expected future cash flows), the market approach (comparing with similar assets, using multiples such as P/E) and the cost approach (the cost to replace it). A stock is usually valued by discounting future dividends or free cash flows, or by comparing multiples with peers.

Intrinsic value is the estimated true worth of an asset based on fundamentals, which may differ from the market price. For a crypto asset, there are no cash flows to discount, so valuation is harder: it relies on network adoption (Metcalfe's law), scarcity and supply, utility, demand and sentiment, and the price is highly speculative. State clearly that crypto valuation is uncertain.

Fundamental analysis estimates the intrinsic value of a company by examining financial statements, earnings, cash flows, management quality, industry position and the economy, to decide whether a stock is under- or overvalued; it is generally used for long-term investing. Technical analysis studies past price and volume data, using charts, patterns and indicators (moving averages, RSI, support and resistance), to forecast short-term price moves, based on the belief that prices reflect all information and that trends repeat.

In short, fundamental analysis asks 'what is it worth?' and technical analysis asks 'where is the price going?'. Many investors combine the two, and critics of technical analysis cite the efficient market hypothesis.

In layman terms, a derivative is a financial contract whose value depends on something else, such as a share, an index, a commodity or a currency. Think of it as a bet or an agreement about the future price, not the asset itself. For example, a farmer can agree today to sell wheat at a fixed price in three months (a forward or futures contract), which protects the farmer from price falls.

The main types are futures and forwards (an obligation to buy or sell at a fixed price on a future date), options (the right but not the obligation to buy or sell) and swaps. They are used for hedging risk, for speculation and for arbitrage, and since they use leverage, they can cause large losses if misused.

This is the standard opener and the panel is judging structure, clarity and confidence. Start with your name and background, and then give a tight summary of about 90 seconds: education, work experience or key achievements, one or two interests, and why you want the MBA.

Example: "I am [name], from [city]. I completed [degree] from [college] and worked as [role] at [company], where I [achievement]. Outside work I [hobby]. I am keen to pursue an MBA to [goal]." Do not recite your resume line by line, and leave two or three hooks that you are comfortable being questioned on.

The panel wants a positive and credible reason for the move. Present it as growth: you went from a large, established FMCG company to a technology company (o9 Solutions, a supply chain and planning software firm) to work closer to analytics, data and technology while using your domain understanding, and to get exposure to many clients and industries.

Example: "At ITC I learned [operations/supply chain/brand management fundamentals]. I moved to o9 because I wanted to work on [planning and analytics solutions] across clients, which has taught me [skills]. This combination of domain and technology is what I want to build on through the MBA." Do not criticise your previous employer.

Prepare a careful, balanced answer. The pandemic hurt cigarette volumes in 2020 through lockdowns, closure of retail outlets and reduced mobility, but recovery was strong afterwards, and ITC's cigarette segment remains its largest profit contributor. Do not quote a specific revenue figure unless you have verified it from the latest annual report.

Volumes do not grow quickly because of high taxation, regulation, health awareness, illicit and cheaper unbranded cigarettes and a stable smoker base, so growth comes mostly from price and mix. Whether it is good to invest is a matter of both returns and ethics: it generates strong cash flows and dividends, but it faces regulatory risks, ESG concerns and exclusion by some funds. ITC has been diversifying into FMCG, hotels, paperboards and agri-business. Offer a balanced view.

Yes, ITC has well-known social initiatives, such as e-Choupal, which links farmers with markets, social investments in watershed development, sustainable agriculture, livelihood programmes and women's empowerment, and a long-standing 'carbon positive, water positive and solid waste recycling positive' claim. These are part of its sustainability agenda.

On whether CSR is good for companies: critics, following Milton Friedman, argue that a business's job is profit and that CSR can be a distraction or a cover for harmful products. Supporters argue that CSR builds trust, brand value, talent and a licence to operate, and reduces long-term risk, and in India, firms above a threshold must spend 2 percent of average net profit on CSR under the Companies Act. A balanced view is that CSR is valuable when it is genuine and linked to the business, but it cannot offset harm caused by the core business.

A balanced answer should describe the last five years in phases. In 2020 the pandemic crash hit markets and GDP, followed by a strong rebound in equities supported by liquidity, low interest rates and retail participation, with a surge in demat accounts and SIP flows. Then in 2022-23 global inflation and rate hikes brought volatility, while India stayed among the fastest-growing major economies, aided by digital payments, infrastructure spending, GST collections and manufacturing initiatives.

Risks include high valuations, inflation, global uncertainty, unemployment and uneven consumption. Say that your view is a general one and name the indicators you track, such as GDP growth, inflation, fiscal deficit and corporate earnings. Verify the latest data before the interview.

The RBI cuts the repo rate mainly when inflation is under control and growth needs support, or when the economy faces a slowdown or external shock. A cut makes borrowing cheaper, which encourages investment and consumption. The impact on the economy is higher credit demand, support for housing, autos and capital goods, and possibly a weaker rupee and, if overdone, higher inflation. For the stock market, a cut generally helps through lower discount rates and a positive sentiment, especially for rate-sensitive sectors like banks, real estate and autos.

If you sell (write) a put option, you receive a premium and take on the obligation to buy the asset at the strike price if the price falls below it. If the market rises or stays flat, you keep the premium; if it falls sharply, losses can be large. So rate cuts that lift the market are generally favourable for a put seller, and the risk is a market fall.

The option premium has two parts, intrinsic value and time value, and it is influenced by the spot price relative to the strike, time to expiry, volatility, interest rates and dividends. In general, a rise in the underlying raises call premiums and lowers put premiums, more time and higher volatility raise both, and the time value decays as expiry nears.

The Greeks measure these sensitivities: delta (change in premium for a change in the underlying price), gamma (change in delta), theta (time decay), vega (sensitivity to volatility) and rho (sensitivity to interest rates). For 'yesterday's impact', only talk about the market move if you actually tracked it; otherwise say honestly that you did not follow it closely, and explain how the move would have affected the premium using the Greeks.

For an at-the-money (ATM) option, delta is roughly 0.5 for a call and roughly -0.5 for a put, in absolute terms about 50 percent. This means that for a Rs 1 move in the underlying, the option premium moves by about Rs 0.50, and it also reflects an approximate 50 percent chance of the option expiring in the money.

Deep in-the-money calls have a delta close to 1, and far out-of-the-money options have a delta near 0. Delta shifts as the underlying moves and as expiry nears, which is captured by gamma.

The panel is asking about a specific share price behaviour, so avoid a definite claim unless you have the latest facts. A structured answer looks at several factors: the stock's valuation and earnings growth compared with peers, the dependence on cigarettes, which have slow volume growth, high taxation and regulatory risk, ESG-driven selling by some investors, the diversification businesses (FMCG, hotels, paperboard, agri) which take time to scale, the demerger of the hotels business and the general market and sector rotation.

Also mention that the share has often given steady returns with dividends rather than sharp rallies, and that at various times it has moved up strongly. Conclude with your view and note that you would check recent results and news before forming a firm opinion.

The panel is asking detailed questions about your work at o9 Solutions, a supply chain planning and analytics platform provider. Be ready to describe in your own words the solution modules you worked on (for example demand planning, supply planning, inventory optimisation and replenishment), a customised solution you delivered, and how you built models: gathering data, defining the planning hierarchy, setting rules and forecasting logic, testing and deployment.

Replenishment means deciding when and how much stock to order or move to meet forecast demand while holding minimum inventory. The factors are demand forecast, lead time, safety stock, service level targets, order quantities and constraints, and cost. On the point that Excel can also do it, the answer is that Excel works for small, simple cases, but platforms handle large data volumes, many SKUs and locations, real-time integration, scenario planning, automation and collaboration. Answer only with what you actually did.

The panel asks about what makes o9 Solutions' approach distinctive. A known feature is its Digital Brain platform, which uses an Enterprise Knowledge Graph (EKG), a graph-based data model that connects data across planning domains (demand, supply, finance and commercial), so that all functions plan on one integrated model with real-time scenario analysis and AI/ML support.

If the 'technical term' they want is the data model, answer 'Enterprise Knowledge Graph' and explain it in a sentence, noting that it differs from traditional relational and siloed planning tools. If you are not certain which term they mean, say what you know and be honest about the limits of your knowledge.

Celebrity endorsement of soft drinks is a debated ethical issue. Arguments that it is unethical: soft drinks have high sugar content linked to obesity, diabetes and dental problems, celebrities influence children and young fans who trust them, and promoting such products may conflict with their role as role models. There is also the concern that endorsement often hides health risks.

Arguments that it is acceptable: the products are legal, endorsements are a standard marketing practice, and consumers have a free choice. Ethical endorsement requires honesty, not making false health claims, avoiding targeting children, and endorsing products the celebrity actually uses. A balanced view is that it is not unethical in itself, but celebrities should practise due diligence and responsibility, and some choose to refuse products they find harmful.

The panel is moving on to ask about your organisation. Describe it concisely: the company's name, industry, size and main products or services, where it stands in the market, and where you fit in, with one or two interesting facts.

A sample: "I work at [company], which is a [type] company in [industry], known for [products]. It has around [number] employees and operates in [markets]. I work in the [team] as [role], where I [responsibility]." Keep the facts accurate. The opening phrase from the panel suggests that you had given an answer they challenged, so stay calm and move forward confidently.

This is a simple factual question. Answer with your college and university, degree and branch, and year of graduation, in one sentence, such as "I graduated from [college], [university], in [year] with a [degree] in [branch]."

If the panel follows up, be ready with a line on what you liked about the college, such as faculty, projects or activities. Keep it short, confident and consistent with your application form.

The panel wants to understand your current role. Give your designation, the team, the main two or three responsibilities, who you work with, and one achievement with a number.

Example: "My work profile is [designation] in [team], where I [main duties]. I coordinate with [stakeholders] and have [achievement, such as reduced cost or improved turnaround time by X percent]." Use simple language that a person outside your industry can follow, and be ready for follow-up questions on any detail.

The panel is testing structured problem solving. A good approach is to follow a clear sequence. First, define what efficiency means (cost per unit, time, output per hour, quality, utilisation). Second, map the current process and collect data to find bottlenecks, waste and delays, for example through value stream mapping. Third, analyse root causes using tools such as the 5 Whys, Pareto analysis and fishbone diagrams. Fourth, implement improvements such as removing non-value-adding steps, standardising work, balancing the line, automation, better layout, preventive maintenance and training, using lean and Six Sigma ideas. Finally, measure results, set up controls and continue to improve.

Add that you would involve the people who do the work, since they know where problems are. A real example from your own experience will strengthen the answer.

The answer depends on your company, so tailor it. In general, companies in or around the transport sector are preparing for electrification by investing in EV and battery technology or partnerships, redesigning products and supply chains, building charging infrastructure or partnering with charging providers, training their workforce, adopting government incentives such as FAME and PLI, and planning for new business models such as battery swapping and leasing.

If you do not know your company's specific plans, say what you do know, for example a public announcement or a project you are aware of, and then give your opinion on what the company should do. Be honest instead of inventing details.

Yes. A battery converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy through electrochemical reactions. It has two electrodes, an anode (negative) and a cathode (positive), separated by an electrolyte. During discharge, a chemical reaction at the anode releases electrons, which flow through the external circuit to the cathode, powering the device, while ions move through the electrolyte to complete the circuit.

In rechargeable batteries such as lead-acid and lithium-ion, applying an external current reverses the reaction and restores the chemical energy. The voltage depends on the chemistry, and the capacity (in ampere-hours) depends on how much active material is present.

The panel is asking about your personal contribution. Be specific about what you did, as distinct from what the team did. Use 'I' for your actions and 'we' for the group result, and use action verbs.

A suitable structure: "My role was [responsibility]. I [analysed data/built the model/coordinated with X], which led to [result]." Quantify the impact where possible and mention the tools or methods you used. If the work was a team project, acknowledge the team's role but make your own part clear, without exaggeration, since follow-up questions will test the details.

The panel uses hobbies to see your personality, consistency and depth. Name one to three hobbies that you really pursue, with evidence: how long, what level and what you gained.

Say: "My main hobbies are [hobby 1] and [hobby 2]. I have been [playing/reading/writing] for [years], and recently I [achievement or habit]. It helps me [relax, think creatively, work in a team]." Avoid generic lists such as 'music, movies, travelling', and be ready for detailed follow-up questions on each.

Name a footballer you actually follow, such as Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo, Sunil Chhetri, Kylian Mbappe or whoever you really like, and be ready to explain the choice. The panel is looking at your reasoning and personality, not at the player.

Say: "My favourite footballer is [name]. I admire [him/her] for [quality, such as consistency, leadership, work ethic or humility]. One moment I remember is [match or story]." If possible, link the quality to something you value in work and teamwork, and avoid running down other players.

The panel wants your reasoning for the choice you made. Give two or three real reasons: the player's skill, consistency, leadership, work ethic, how they handled setbacks, or a match that inspired you, and then relate it to a trait you value.

For example: "Because of [quality]. He showed that [lesson], and I try to apply the same attitude to [studies, work, teamwork]." A personal story, such as the match where you first noticed the player, makes the answer more authentic than a list of statistics.

Yes, you should always have one or two good questions, since it shows curiosity and preparation. Do not say 'no questions'. Ask something that cannot be found easily on the website, such as how the programme helps students move into a different function, how industry projects and live cases are integrated, or what traits the panel sees in the most successful students.

Avoid questions about salary guarantees or details already published. Keep it brief and polite, listen to the answer and thank the panel for their time.

They are called machine learning algorithms because they learn patterns from data instead of following explicitly programmed rules. In traditional programming, a developer writes rules to turn inputs into outputs. In machine learning, we give the algorithm examples (data), and it adjusts its internal parameters to improve performance on a task, for example by minimising an error measure, and then applies what it learned to new data.

The 'learning' is the process of improving through experience: supervised learning uses labelled examples (regression, classification), unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering), and reinforcement learning learns from rewards. Use an example, such as a model learning to predict churn from past customers.

Answer honestly. In most cases, candidates use standard algorithms from libraries such as scikit-learn, TensorFlow or PyTorch rather than writing them from scratch. Say precisely what you did: which algorithms you used, how you prepared the data, tuned hyperparameters, evaluated the model and interpreted results, and what, if anything, you implemented yourself.

Example: "I used existing libraries for [algorithms], and my contribution was [data cleaning, feature engineering, model selection and validation]. I understand how [one algorithm] works, and I can explain it." Never claim you wrote something from scratch if you did not, and be ready to explain the logic of at least one algorithm.

The panel is testing why you chose product management and whether you understand it. A good answer shows that you know what a product manager does: define the problem and vision, understand users, prioritise features, work with engineering, design and business teams, and take responsibility for outcomes.

Example: "I want to become a Product Manager because I enjoy [understanding user problems and working across teams]. In my role at [company], I [experience linked to product, such as owning a feature, working with customers or analysing usage data]. An MBA will add [business strategy, finance and marketing] to my technical background." Show a real link between your experience and the role.

A product manager (PM) is responsible for the success of a product across its life cycle. The PM identifies customer problems and market opportunities, defines the product vision and strategy, prioritises features and creates the roadmap, works with engineering, design, marketing, sales and support to deliver it, defines success metrics and tracks them, and decides what to build and what not to build.

The PM is often described as the 'CEO of the product', though without direct authority, so influence, communication and data-driven decision-making are key. A good answer adds an example, such as how a PM would handle a request to add a feature.

A product is shut down when it no longer makes sense to continue. Typical triggers are declining usage and revenue with no sign of recovery, a poor fit with the company's strategy, high maintenance cost compared with the value it delivers, the product being replaced by a better one, technological obsolescence, regulatory or legal problems, or failing to reach product-market fit after repeated attempts.

A good PM looks at data (retention, revenue, cost, customer feedback), tests alternatives such as a pivot or relaunch, and then plans the shutdown responsibly: communicating to customers, offering migration paths, supporting existing users and reallocating the team. The decision should be based on facts, not emotional attachment.

NBFCs, or Non-Banking Financial Companies, are companies registered under the Companies Act and regulated by the Reserve Bank of India that provide financial services such as loans, leasing, hire purchase, asset financing and investments, but do not hold a banking licence. They cannot accept demand deposits or issue cheques drawn on themselves, and they are not part of the payment and settlement system in the same way as banks.

They are important in India for reaching customers that banks may not serve, such as small businesses, vehicle buyers, housing finance seekers and rural borrowers. Examples are Bajaj Finance, Muthoot Finance and Shriram Finance. Their risk is that they depend on market borrowing, so liquidity stress can affect them quickly.

Yes, the major NBFC crisis began in 2018 with the default of IL&FS, a large infrastructure financier, which triggered a liquidity crunch because many NBFCs relied on short-term borrowing from debt markets and mutual funds to fund long-term assets, creating an asset-liability mismatch. It was followed by trouble at DHFL and other lenders, and later the Yes Bank rescue in 2020, which further tightened credit.

The RBI and the government responded with liquidity support, partial credit guarantee schemes, stricter regulation (the scale-based regulatory framework for NBFCs) and better governance and disclosure norms. Mention the lessons: asset-liability management, governance and the risk of over-leveraging. Check your facts before the interview.

Banks fail mainly because of problems in managing risk and trust. The common reasons are poor credit decisions leading to large non-performing assets, asset-liability mismatches, concentration of lending in a few borrowers or sectors, fraud and weak governance, lack of liquidity during a run (loss of depositor confidence), excessive risk-taking or leverage, and macroeconomic shocks or interest rate changes.

Because banks hold only a fraction of deposits as reserves, a loss of confidence can quickly become fatal, as with Lehman Brothers in 2008 and Silicon Valley Bank in 2023 and in India's Yes Bank and PMC Bank cases. Regulation, capital adequacy requirements, deposit insurance and supervision exist to reduce such risks.

The panel is pointing out that privatisation does not guarantee good outcomes. A fair answer accepts this. Privatisation can improve efficiency, accountability and customer service through profit motives and competition, but private banks and NBFCs can still fail because of risk-taking, weak governance, poor credit appraisal, concentration risk, fraud and excessive leverage, and business cycles. Failure does not need corruption, as bad management and misjudged risk are enough.

The main point is that ownership is not the only factor, and what matters is strong regulation, supervision, transparency, capital buffers and good governance in any bank, public or private. Mention examples such as Yes Bank or Lakshmi Vilas Bank among private banks, and acknowledge that public sector banks have also had their problems.

The panel uses hobbies to see your personality, consistency and depth. Name one to three hobbies that you really pursue, with evidence: how long, what level and what you gained.

Say: "My main hobbies are [hobby 1] and [hobby 2]. I have been [playing/reading/writing] for [years], and recently I [achievement or habit]. It helps me [relax, think creatively, work in a team]." Avoid generic lists such as 'music, movies, travelling', and be ready for detailed follow-up questions on each. If you mention reading, be ready to talk about one book in detail.

The panel is checking whether your interest in product management is backed by learning. Name only books you have actually read, and be ready to discuss ideas. Well-known titles include 'Inspired' by Marty Cagan, 'The Lean Startup' by Eric Ries, 'Cracking the PM Interview' by Gayle McDowell and Jackie Bavaro, 'Hooked' by Nir Eyal and 'Sprint' by Jake Knapp.

Example: "I have read [book], and the idea that stayed with me was [insight, such as building to validate assumptions or focusing on outcomes rather than outputs], which I applied when [example]." If you have not read any, say so honestly, mention blogs, case studies or podcasts you follow, and say what you plan to read.

This is a warm-up question to put you at ease, and the panel is observing your tone and composure. Answer naturally and briefly: "I am doing well, sir, thank you. How are you?" Smile and keep eye contact.

Do not give a long explanation about nerves or the journey. A short, polite and confident reply sets a positive tone, and the panel will move to the real questions.

The panel is asking about the company you work for, Adobe. Give a short, positive and honest view of the company and of your experience there: its products (Creative Cloud, Acrobat and PDF, Experience Cloud), its work culture, learning opportunities and what you enjoy.

Example: "Adobe is a great place to work. It has a strong product culture, and I have learnt [skills] working on [project]. It has also made me curious about [business side], which is why I want an MBA." Do not criticise your employer, and tie the answer back to your motivation for the MBA.

The panel is joking or probing a seeming contradiction: you say the company is great, but you are here for an MBA. Respond calmly with a light tone and clarity: leaving does not mean dissatisfaction; it reflects a desire for growth beyond the current path.

A sample: "It is possible because it is a great organisation that has taught me a lot, and I want to build further on that. The MBA is the next step to broaden my skills in [business/strategy/finance], and I hope to return to roles such as product management where I can use both." Show gratitude, avoid defensiveness and reinforce your goal.

Adobe's annual revenue is in the range of about 20 billion US dollars in recent years, driven by its Digital Media (Creative Cloud and Document Cloud) and Digital Experience segments, though the exact figure depends on the fiscal year. It is safest to say 'roughly 20 billion dollars, with most coming from subscriptions' and add that you would check the latest annual report for the precise number.

If you are asked about trends, you can say that growth has come from the shift to a subscription model, which provides recurring revenue, and from the expansion into digital experience and AI-powered features.

Adobe has roughly 30,000 employees worldwide in recent years, with major offices in San Jose, California, and large operations in India (Noida and Bengaluru), though the exact number changes by year. It is better to give an approximate figure and say that you do not remember the exact number than to state a precise one.

If you work there, you can add your office location and, if you know it, how large the India team is.

A reasoned answer is better than a definite one. Amazon, through the Kindle devices and store, has dominated the dedicated e-reader and e-book market with its own ecosystem and large catalogue. Adobe is not mainly a seller of e-readers, but it owns the PDF standard and the Acrobat and Adobe Digital Editions ecosystem, so it plays an important role in document and e-publishing tools. Microsoft is more of a platform and productivity player and is not a leading force in e-readers.

On this basis, Amazon is winning the consumer e-reading market, while Adobe leads in the PDF and document workflow space, so they compete in different parts of the market. State your assumptions, and give your view with reasons.

The question asks you to define your target market for your product. Answer by segmenting: who the customers are (individuals, students, professionals, enterprises), what problem they have, where they are and how big the segment is. Use a simple structure of the target segment, their needs and why they would choose your product over alternatives.

For example, for a document or creative product: "Our core market is [creative professionals, businesses and students] who need [reliable document workflows, creative tools], and the biggest segment by revenue is [enterprise and subscription users]." Tie it to your actual product and role, and avoid vague terms like 'everyone'.

Not necessarily an expert, but a product manager needs financial literacy. A PM should be able to read a P&L and understand revenue, margins, cost structure, unit economics, customer acquisition cost, lifetime value and the business case for a feature, since prioritisation decisions need to be justified with numbers.

However, a PM does not have to be an accountant or finance specialist; the finance team handles detailed reporting. The core skills are customer insight, prioritisation, communication and analytical thinking. A balanced answer is that financial understanding is a requirement for good decisions, and that an MBA helps to strengthen it.

The panel is asking about a recent news item involving the company you work for. If you know the news, summarise it briefly and neutrally: what happened, why it matters and what it means for the company and customers. If you are not aware of the item, say so honestly: "Sir, I am not aware of the latest developments between the two companies, but I would like to read about it."

Avoid guessing. Because you work at Adobe, the panel expects you to be updated on company news, so it is wise to scan the latest headlines about your company before the interview.

Modern OCR (optical character recognition) systems often use neural networks, but OCR is not based only on them. Traditional OCR used image processing, pattern matching and feature extraction (such as template matching, zoning and classifiers like SVM or k-NN). Modern systems use deep learning, with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract visual features and recurrent networks or transformers (for example LSTM and CTC models) to read sequences of characters, which gives much better accuracy on handwriting, varied fonts and noisy images.

So the answer is that many current OCR engines, such as Tesseract 4 and later or cloud OCR services, are neural network-based, though older rule-based approaches exist.

This is a follow-up asking you to explain something again, probably in a simpler or clearer way. Take a moment to think, and restate the concept in plain language using an analogy or an example, assuming the listener is not an expert.

A good structure is: a one-line summary, a simple analogy, a step-by-step explanation and a short real-world use. For example, for OCR you could say: "It is like teaching a computer to read printed text: it looks at the image, finds the shapes of letters, and matches them to characters, and neural networks make this reading more accurate." Check whether the panel needs more detail after your explanation.

The panel is challenging a seemingly redundant move. Do not downplay your academics. Explain that your academic strength shows your ability to learn, but your goals need skills that technical or academic education alone does not give: business strategy, finance, leadership, managing people and cross-functional decision-making.

Example: "My academics have given me a strong analytical base, but I want to move from [solving technical problems] to [leading and making business decisions]. For that I need [finance, strategy, people management] and the exposure that an MBA offers." Link it to a clear goal, and avoid sounding boastful.

The panel is making a provocative remark to test your composure and ethics. Stay calm and respectful, and do not get defensive. Correct the premise gently: ITC is a diversified company, and your work is about [packaging and printing technology/operations], where a mechanical engineering background applies directly. Also, tobacco is a legal product with regulatory oversight, and the company is a large employer, taxpayer and diversifier.

A sample: "Sir, I understand the concern. I work in [packaging/operations], where I apply my engineering skills to [process and quality improvement]. ITC is a diversified business, and the cigarette business is legal and heavily regulated. At the same time, I am conscious of the health issues, which is also part of why I want to build skills for [broader roles]." Show maturity, not defensiveness.

The panel is clarifying your role. Confirm accurately: if you work in packaging, explain that your division supplies packaging materials to ITC's various businesses, including cigarettes and also foods, personal care and others, and describe your role in a neutral and factual tone.

Example: "Yes, part of our output goes to the cigarette business, but the packaging unit also supplies [foods and other products]. My role is [process/quality/operations], which focuses on [efficiency, quality, cost]." Do not hide facts or become defensive, and be ready for the ethical follow-up that usually comes next.

This is an ethics question, and the panel wants to see a thoughtful and honest answer, not defensiveness. Acknowledge the concern: smoking is harmful, and the debate is legitimate. Then give your reasoning: tobacco is a legal product, strictly regulated and heavily taxed, adults have the freedom to choose, the industry provides livelihoods and revenue to the government, and many companies, including ITC, are diversifying away from tobacco and into other businesses.

Also show your own values: you take the health issue seriously, you believe in responsible business practices, and your personal contribution is in a professional role. A balanced conclusion is that it is a fair ethical question, and that your view is that companies should minimise harm, comply with regulations and invest in alternative growth areas. Avoid a rigid defence or a harsh attack on your employer.

This is a tough follow-up that concerns involuntary exposure. Be honest and sensitive: a passive smoker has little choice, and that is the strongest argument for regulation. This is why India has banned smoking in public places under COTPA (2003) and restricts advertising, and why public health measures focus on separating smokers from non-smokers.

An answer could be: "Sir, you are right, a passive smoker has little choice, and that is why strict rules on smoking in public places are essential. Adults can make personal choices, but those choices should not harm others, and I support strong enforcement of such laws." This shows ethical awareness and respect for the other person's view.

The panel is making a good point that addiction reduces free choice. A thoughtful answer agrees partly: nicotine is addictive, so the choice is often made only at the start, which is why prevention, regulation and awareness matter, such as warnings on packs, age restrictions, taxation, advertising bans and cessation support.

Say: "I agree that addiction limits choice, which is why the real choice happens at the beginning, and why society must focus on preventing young people from starting, and on helping those addicted to quit." This shows that you understand the issue and support responsible policy, without defending harm. Stay calm and respectful throughout.

Yes. E-cigarettes (vapes) are battery-powered devices that heat a liquid (e-liquid, usually with nicotine, propylene glycol, glycerine and flavourings) to create an aerosol that the user inhales, without burning tobacco. They were marketed as a less harmful alternative to smoking and as an aid to quitting.

However, concerns include nicotine addiction, appeal to young people through flavours, and lung injury and other health risks. India banned the production, import, sale and advertising of e-cigarettes through the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act, 2019. Present a balanced view, and mention that regulation differs from country to country.

The scientific view is that e-cigarettes are likely to be less harmful than conventional cigarettes for adult smokers who switch completely, because they do not involve burning tobacco, which produces tar and many toxic chemicals. However, they are not harmless: they deliver nicotine, which is addictive, and long-term health effects are still not fully known. There are also concerns about youth uptake, flavours and lung injuries, and many people use both products, which weakens the benefit.

This is why health bodies are cautious, and India has banned them. A balanced answer is that they may be less harmful than smoking but are not safe, especially for non-smokers and young people.

The panel wants an honest and positive description of your current job. Say what you like and what you have learnt (responsibility, working with teams, technical depth, exposure to business), and also mention what you want to grow into, which leads naturally to the MBA.

Example: "I find it challenging and rewarding. I have learnt [skills], and I enjoy [aspect]. At the same time, I see the need to build [broader business skills], which is why I am here." Avoid complaining about your employer or showing dissatisfaction, since it reflects poorly.

This follow-up tests the consistency of your reasons. Acknowledge what you have learnt, and explain that this learning has revealed the gap: you have understood [operations/technology/the shop floor] deeply, but to move into roles with broader responsibility such as [management or strategy], you need structured knowledge of finance, marketing, strategy and leadership, and the MBA is the best way to gain it.

A sample: "I have learnt a lot, and it showed me the limits of my current skill set. I want to complement my technical learning with business skills to grow into [role]." Keep it positive and specific, and tie it to a clear goal.

The panel is questioning why you are leaving so early. Be honest about the short tenure and do not make excuses. Explain that although you valued the experience, you are clear about your goals, and in seven months you learnt what you needed about [the industry/the function] and realised that your growth requires an MBA. Show that you gave the job a proper effort and that the decision is not impulsive.

Example: "In seven months I gained [experience], and it also made me realise that I want to move into [area], for which I need the MBA. I would rather start my MBA now so that I can apply it for a longer career." Do not criticise the company, and show that your goals are consistent.

The panel has given you a practical exercise on a company's share price and a question on GST. For the graph, draw a simple price-versus-time line chart, with the date on the horizontal axis and share price on the vertical, and mark key events such as results announcements, the market crash or rally, and policy events. Draw only what you actually know, and state that your sketch is approximate.

GST (Goods and Services Tax) was implemented in India on 1 July 2017, replacing many central and state indirect taxes with one unified tax. If the question involves a recent year, mention what you know and verify the market data beforehand. Take your time, think aloud and label your axes.

The panel is asking you to explain a price rise after an event, and the answer depends on the stock in question. A structured way to answer is to separate possible factors: company-specific (strong results, margins, new products, dividends, management announcements), sector factors (demand, regulation, taxes) and market-wide factors (liquidity, interest rates, foreign inflows, overall sentiment).

If the event was GST implementation, you could argue that it removed tax cascading and simplified compliance for many companies, which improved sentiment, and that organised players gained market share from the unorganised sector. State that markets reflect expectations, and that you are giving reasoned views rather than certain explanations.

The panel wants your view on the recent movement of the share price. Be careful: unless you have checked recent data, do not state precise figures. Explain the possible drivers of short-term moves: results or news about the company, sector developments, global markets, foreign institutional investor flows, interest rate expectations and the broad market trend.

A good approach is to say: "Over the past week the stock has [moved up/down/stayed range-bound], which I think was driven by [reason]. I would look at the news flow and sector trend before drawing a conclusion." If you did not track it, honestly say so and show how you would analyse it. Before an interview, check the recent price chart of your company.

This question usually follows a mention of a city, country or campus where you studied or worked, and the panel wants to see how you adapt to new environments. Describe the place briefly and honestly: the culture, the people, the biggest adjustment you had to make, and one thing you learnt from it.

Keep the tone positive and specific rather than generic. For example: "It was challenging at first because of [language/food/climate], but it taught me independence and how to work with people from different backgrounds." Avoid complaining about the place or the people.

The panel is probing the difference between playing and leading. Clarify your exact role: as a player you focused on your own performance, while as a captain or manager you planned, motivated, resolved conflicts and took responsibility for results. Say it honestly if you held both roles.

Give one example where wearing both hats helped, such as understanding teammates' problems because you played alongside them, and one trade-off, such as finding it hard to be objective. This shows self-awareness and leadership maturity.

Managing a multicultural team tests your people skills and emotional intelligence. A good answer covers three things: first, understanding differences in communication style, language, food, festivals and work habits; second, setting common goals and simple shared rules so everyone felt included; third, using formal and informal bonding, such as team lunches or sports, to build trust.

Back it with one real example of a misunderstanding you resolved. Conclude with what you learnt, for instance that listening before judging and over-communicating clearly are the keys to leading diverse teams.

This is a simple factual follow-up, so answer directly and honestly. If the team members did not know English well, explain how you communicated, for example through simple words, gestures, translation help, written instructions, visuals or a common language such as Hindi or the local language.

If they did know English, say so briefly and mention any differences in accent or fluency. The panel wants to see that you can overcome communication barriers without making a big drama of it, and that you stay truthful about your abilities.

This looks like a question about a football formation (for example 4-1-2-3). Be ready to explain why you chose it. A formation is the way a team spreads its players on the field: four defenders, one holding midfielder, two central midfielders and three forwards. The panel wants to see strategic thinking, not football trivia.

Explain that you chose it to balance defence and attack, to exploit your players' strengths, and to adapt to the opponent. Connect it to business: just as a team structure is designed around strengths and goals, an organisation structures roles to meet strategy.

In a formation like 4-1-2-3 the single '1' is the holding or defensive midfielder, a role that sits in front of the defenders. This player shields the defence, breaks up opposition attacks, and distributes the ball to the more attacking midfielders and forwards. It is the link between defence and attack.

You can draw the management parallel: this role is like a middle manager or operations head who protects the core while enabling the front line to perform. If you played this position yourself, say what you learnt about discipline, positioning and supporting others.

This is a follow-up question, so the panel is checking whether your earlier statement holds up under probing. Answer from your own real experience in two or three crisp sentences, and avoid contradicting anything you said before.

If you met Chinese students at VIT, say honestly yes or no. If yes, describe how you interacted, what you noticed about their study habits, and one learning. If not, say so and mention the international exposure you did get. Never exaggerate cross-cultural experience, as the panel may probe further.

This is a follow-up question, so the panel is checking whether your earlier statement holds up under probing. Answer from your own real experience in two or three crisp sentences, and avoid contradicting anything you said before.

If the question is about foreign classmates, describe them with respect and specific observations, such as hard-working, disciplined, friendly or reserved at first, rather than stereotypes. Mention one concrete interaction that shows you can work with people from other cultures. Avoid sweeping generalisations about a nationality.

The panel wants a thoughtful, non-defensive answer. Reasons international students come to India include lower cost of education and living, English-medium instruction, strong engineering and IT programmes, exposure to a large and diverse country, scholarships, and the global reputation of certain Indian institutions. Students also often value study abroad for the experience itself, regardless of local university quality.

Be respectful: acknowledge that every country has strong universities and that students choose based on cost, course, visa and career goals. Avoid any political comment or national comparisons that sound boastful.

This is a follow-up question, so the panel is checking whether your earlier statement holds up under probing. Answer from your own real experience in two or three crisp sentences, and avoid contradicting anything you said before.

Answer truthfully whether your team had Chinese members. If not, you can explain that team selection was based on local participation, interest and skill, and mention what diversity your team did have. Keep it short and neutral and do not invent details.

This question invites a stereotype, so be balanced and careful. Many Chinese and other international students are indeed strong in programming and mathematics, but skill varies by individual, and it is wrong to generalise by nationality. Strong coding comes from practice, education systems that emphasise fundamentals, and personal interest.
